references.authors: Almeida FN, Leray C, Albignac M, et al.
references.title: Py-GC-MS/MS quantification of microplastics in vertebrate tissues: Addressing false positives of polyethylene
references.finding: Lipid interference causes polyethylene false positives in Py-GC/MS of tissue; markers with carbon chains longer than common lipids were needed to separate them.

references.authors: Braun JM, Smith KW, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: Variability of urinary phthalate metabolite and bisphenol A concentrations before and during pregnancy
references.finding: During pregnancy ICCs were 0.50 for MEP, 0.45 for MBP, 0.25 for MBzP, 0.12 for BPA and 0.08 for sum-DEHP; one spot sample adequately classified MEP and MBP but not DEHP or BPA.

references.authors: Buckley JP, Pacyga DC, Xun X, et al.
references.title: Gestational Exposure to 10 Classes of Priority Chemicals and Birth Outcomes in the ECHO Cohort
references.finding: Among 113 analytes in 10 chemical classes, several phthalates and alternative plasticizers were linked to slightly shorter gestation; summed DiNP metabolites: 0.6 days shorter, preterm birth OR 1.16 per IQR.

references.authors: Castellini C, Muselli M, Parisi A, et al.
references.title: Association between urinary bisphenol A concentrations and semen quality: A meta-analytic study
references.finding: Urinary BPA was only weakly associated with lower sperm motility, and the association disappeared after correction for publication bias; authors judge the link clinically negligible, if any.

references.authors: Cox KD, Covernton GA, Davies HL, et al.
references.title: Human Consumption of Microplastics
references.finding: Estimated annual microplastic consumption of 39,000-52,000 particles, rising to 74,000-121,000 with inhalation.

references.authors: Cui C, Guo Z, Liu Y, et al.
references.title: Tissue-specific distribution of microplastics in human blood and carotid plaques: A paired sample analysis
references.finding: Paired blood and plaque Py-GC/MS found mean 75 ug/g in blood and 433 ug/g in plaque with only moderate correlation between them (r 0.30).

references.authors: Due I, Rubio L, Catalán J, et al.
references.title: Mammalian reproductive and developmental toxicity of micro- and nanoplastics: a critical appraisal of evidence using the SciRAP tool
references.finding: SciRAP appraisal: of mammalian reproductive/developmental micro/nanoplastic studies only 7 were strong for risk assessment; particle characterization, dose and dose-response were often missing.

references.authors: European Commission
references.title: Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/3190 of 19 December 2024 on the use of bisphenol A (BPA) and other bisphenols and bisphenol derivatives in materials and articles intended to come into contact with food
references.journal: Official Journal of the European Union
references.finding: Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/3190 bans BPA and its salts in food contact materials (plastics, coatings, varnishes, inks, adhesives, rubbers), with an 18-month transition to 20 July 2026 for most single-use items and 36 months (to 20 January 2028) for some uses; other hazardous bisphenols need authorization.

references.authors: Galloway TS, Baglin N, Lee BP, et al.
references.title: An engaged research study to assess the effect of a 'real-world' dietary intervention on urinary bisphenol A (BPA) levels in teenagers
references.finding: A self-designed 7-day diet to avoid BPA did not lower urinary BPA overall (p=0.25); participants found BPA-free food hard to identify and unlikely to sustain.

references.authors: Génard-Walton M, Warembourg C, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: Using mixture and exposome methods to assess the associations and interactions of chemical biomarkers with semen parameters
references.finding: Across four mixture/exposome models of 24 biomarkers (BPA, parabens, triclosan, 17 phthalate metabolites, hair mercury), the consistent signals were mercury (positive) and triclosan (negative); the overall mixture had small, imprecise associations with semen parameters.

references.authors: Goldstone AE, Chen Z, Perry MJ, et al.
references.title: Urinary bisphenol A and semen quality, the LIFE Study
references.finding: In a general-population preconception cohort, urinary BPA was not associated with 34 of 35 semen measures; the only significant finding was less sperm DNA fragmentation with higher BPA.

references.authors: Guo Y, Rong M, Fan Y, et al.
references.title: The Presence of Microplastics in Human Semen and Their Associations with Semen Quality
references.finding: Microplastics (LD-IR) were found in 34 of 45 semen samples; men with PET particles had lower progressive motility (20.6 vs 34.9%, p=0.056); no link with concentration or count.

references.authors: Harray AJ, Lucas AD, Herrmann SE, et al.
references.title: Low-plastic diet and urinary levels of plastic-associated phthalates and bisphenols: the randomized controlled PERTH Trial
references.finding: A 7-day diet of food sourced to minimize plastic contact, with plastic-free kitchenware and personal-care products, cut urinary MnBP by 37.5%, MBzP by 53.5% and BPA by 59.7% vs no intervention; personal-care swaps alone lowered MnBP; Minderoo-funded.

references.authors: Hauser R, Meeker JD, Singh NP, et al.
references.title: DNA damage in human sperm is related to urinary levels of phthalate monoester and oxidative metabolites
references.finding: MEP was associated with more neutral-Comet sperm DNA damage; MEHP was associated only after adjusting for the oxidative metabolite MEHHP (Comet extent +17.3%, tail % +17.5% per IQR).

references.authors: Hauser R, Gaskins AJ, Souter I, et al.
references.title: Urinary Phthalate Metabolite Concentrations and Reproductive Outcomes among Women Undergoing in Vitro Fertilization: Results from the EARTH Study
references.finding: Women in the top vs bottom quartile of urinary DEHP metabolites had fewer and fewer mature oocytes and 19 percentage points lower clinical pregnancy and live birth per cycle.

references.authors: Hernandez LM, Xu EG, Larsson HCE, et al.
references.title: Plastic Teabags Release Billions of Microparticles and Nanoparticles into Tea
references.finding: Steeping one plastic teabag at 95 C released about 11.6 billion microplastic and 3.1 billion nanoplastic particles into a cup.

references.authors: Hu CJ, Garcia MA, Nihart A, et al.
references.title: Microplastic presence in dog and human testis and its potential association with sperm count and weights of testis and epididymis
references.finding: Py-GC/MS found microplastics in every testis (mean 328 ug/g in humans, mostly polyethylene), with polymer-specific negative correlations with sperm count in dogs.

references.authors: Hu CJ, Garcia MA, Nihart A, et al.
references.title: Response to comment on: "Microplastic presence in dog and human testis and its potential association with sperm count and weights of testis and epididymis"
references.finding: Authors' response to the comment on the testis microplastics study.

references.authors: Hussain KA, Romanova S, Okur I, et al.
references.title: Assessing the Release of Microplastics and Nanoplastics from Plastic Containers and Reusable Food Pouches: Implications for Human Health
references.finding: Microwaving some plastic containers released up to 4.22 million microplastic and 2.11 billion nanoplastic particles per cm2 of plastic in 3 minutes.

references.authors: Ilki FY
references.title: Increased seminal microplastic burden in men with varicocele: a controlled clinical study
references.finding: Light-microscopy counts found more seminal microplastics in varicocele (median 8 vs 4 particles/mL); microplastic load correlated with lower concentration, motility and morphology.

references.authors: Kiwitt-Cárdenas J, Adoamnei E, Arense-Gonzalo JJ, et al.
references.title: Associations between urinary concentrations of bisphenol A and sperm DNA fragmentation in young men
references.finding: No association between urinary BPA and sperm DNA fragmentation overall; a positive association only in the subgroup with SDF above 30%.

references.authors: Kong F, Fang L, Gui Y, et al.
references.title: Polyethylene and Polyvinyl Chloride Nanoplastics in Human Follicular Fluid and Seminal Plasma: Impact on Fertilization and Sperm Quality
references.finding: Py-GC/MS found polyethylene and PVC nanoplastics in follicular fluid and seminal plasma; higher follicular PE/PVC tertiles had lower fertilization rates and seminal PVC tracked lower motility, but neither was linked to implantation or pregnancy.

references.authors: Lane T, de Ruijter VN, Wardani I, et al.
references.title: A QA/QC screening framework to assess studies reporting microplastic presence in human organs, tissues, and bodily fluids
references.finding: QA/QC screen of human-tissue microplastic studies: none met all essential criteria; common gaps in sample representativeness, positive controls and blank documentation.

references.authors: Machtinger R, Gaskins AJ, Racowsky C, et al.
references.title: Urinary concentrations of biomarkers of phthalates and phthalate alternatives and IVF outcomes
references.finding: Higher DEHP metabolites were linked to fewer total, mature and fertilized oocytes and top-quality embryos, but no phthalate metabolite was linked to implantation, clinical pregnancy or live birth; DINCH metabolites showed no associations.

references.authors: Marfella R, Prattichizzo F, Sardu C, et al.
references.title: Microplastics and Nanoplastics in Atheromas and Cardiovascular Events
references.finding: Patients with detectable micro/nanoplastics (mainly polyethylene, PVC) in carotid plaque had a higher risk of MI, stroke or death over 34 months (HR 4.53, 2.00-10.27).

references.authors: Marfella R, Prattichizzo F
references.title: Microplastics and Nanoplastics in Atheromas. Reply
references.finding: Authors' reply to several NEJM letters questioning contamination control, confounding and measurement in the plaque-microplastics cohort.

references.authors: Martínez Steele E, Khandpur N, da Costa Louzada ML, et al.
references.title: Association between dietary contribution of ultra-processed foods and urinary concentrations of phthalates and bisphenol in a nationally representative sample of the US population aged 6 years and older
references.finding: Urinary DiNP, mCNP, mCPP, MBzP and BPF rose monotonically across quintiles of ultra-processed food intake.

references.authors: Meeker JD, Ehrlich S, Toth TL, et al.
references.title: Semen quality and sperm DNA damage in relation to urinary bisphenol A among men from an infertility clinic
references.finding: An IQR rise in urinary BPA was linked to 23% lower sperm concentration, 13% lower normal morphology and 10% more Comet tail DNA.

references.authors: Mínguez-Alarcón L, Gaskins AJ, Chiu YH, et al.
references.title: Urinary bisphenol A concentrations and association with in vitro fertilization outcomes among women from a fertility clinic
references.finding: In the expanded Boston cohort, urinary BPA was not associated with peak estradiol, fertilization, embryo quality, implantation, clinical pregnancy or live birth.

references.authors: Mok-Lin E, Ehrlich S, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: Urinary bisphenol A concentrations and ovarian response among women undergoing IVF
references.finding: Each log-unit increase in urinary BPA was associated with 12% fewer oocytes retrieved and 213 pg/mL lower peak estradiol.

references.authors: A Monikh F, Materić D, Valsami-Jones E, et al.
references.title: Challenges in studying microplastics in human brain
references.finding: Letter from analytical chemists setting out challenges in measuring microplastics in human brain, including Py-GC/MS interference.

references.authors: Nihart AJ, Garcia MA, El Hayek E, et al.
references.title: Bioaccumulation of microplastics in decedent human brains
references.n: decedent brain, liver and kidney samples
references.finding: Pyrolysis GC/MS, infrared and electron microscopy reported micro/nanoplastics, mainly polyethylene, in human liver, kidney and brain, with higher proportions of polyethylene in brain.

references.authors: Nihart AJ, Garcia MA, El Hayek E, et al.
references.title: Author Correction: Bioaccumulation of microplastics in decedent human brains
references.finding: Author correction to the decedent-brain microplastics paper.

references.authors: Qian N, Gao X, Lang X, et al.
references.title: Rapid single-particle chemical imaging of nanoplastics by SRS microscopy
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Single-particle SRS imaging estimated about 240,000 micro/nanoplastic particles per litre of bottled water, about 90% nanoplastics.

references.authors: Qu J, Zeng J, Mou L, et al.
references.title: Plastic tableware use, microplastic accumulation, and sperm quality: from epidemiological evidence to FOXA1/p38 mechanistic insights
references.finding: Microplastics were detected in 55.5% of semen samples; frequent plastic-tableware use tracked semen microplastics, and microplastics with lower concentration only in a subgroup (BMI <24, frequent use).

references.authors: Rauert C, Charlton N, Bagley A, et al.
references.title: Assessing the Efficacy of Pyrolysis-Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry for Nanoplastic and Microplastic Analysis in Human Blood
references.finding: Py-GC/MS polyethylene and PVC signals in blood suffer matrix false positives; realistic detection limits were up to 20 times higher than nominal and no polymer other than interfered PE exceeded them.

references.authors: Sathyanarayana S, Alcedo G, Saelens BE, et al.
references.title: Unexpected results in a randomized dietary trial to reduce phthalate and bisphenol A exposures
references.finding: A 5-day catered 'low-exposure' diet unexpectedly raised urinary DEHP metabolites (to an estimated intake above EPA and EFSA limits for children) because ingredients such as ground coriander and milk were contaminated.

references.authors: Uppu RM, Peijnenburg W, Hays SM
references.title: Comment on: "Microplastic presence in dog and human testis and its potential association with sperm count and weights of testis and epididymis"
references.finding: Published comment arguing the testis microplastics study lacked adequate blanks, controls and method validation.

references.authors: Vernet C, Philippat C, Agier L, et al.
references.title: An Empirical Validation of the Within-subject Biospecimens Pooling Approach to Minimize Exposure Misclassification in Biomarker-based Studies
references.n: 16 pregnant women (all voids, several weeks) plus simulation
references.finding: One spot urine sample produced 69% attenuation bias in a BPA dose-response; about 18 samples were needed to bring bias down to 10%.

references.authors: Wang Q, Chi F, Liu Y, et al.
references.title: Polyethylene microplastic exposure adversely affects oocyte quality in human and mouse
references.finding: Polyethylene was the most common microplastic in follicular fluid (86%) and correlated with lower fertilization rate (r -0.41); PE-exposed mice had fewer and poorer-quality oocytes and more ROS.

references.authors: Wang H, He H, Wei Y, et al.
references.title: Do phthalates and their metabolites cause poor semen quality? A systematic review and meta-analysis of epidemiological studies on risk of decline in sperm quality
references.finding: Urinary MBP (pooled OR 2.19) and MBzP (OR 1.88) and semen DEHP (r -0.23) were associated with low sperm concentration; no significant links with motility or morphology or for MEP and other metabolites.

references.authors: Wehrli L, Martin OV, Trasande L, et al.
references.title: Reproductive toxicity of micro- and nanoplastics: Insights from experimental and human studies
references.finding: Scoping review: micro/nanoplastics found in reproductive tissues and fluids; 30 animal studies report altered semen, folliculogenesis or litter size; particle vs additive effects cannot be separated.

references.authors: Welch BM, Keil AP, Buckley JP, et al.
references.title: Associations Between Prenatal Urinary Biomarkers of Phthalate Exposure and Preterm Birth: A Pooled Study of 16 US Cohorts
references.finding: Each interquartile-range rise in urinary MBP, MiBP, MECPP or MCPP across pregnancy was linked to 12-16% higher odds of preterm birth; modelled 30% and 50% cuts in the phthalate mixture would prevent about 6 and 11 preterm births per 1,000 live births.

references.authors: Yang TC, Jovanovic N, Chong F, et al.
references.title: Interventions to Reduce Exposure to Synthetic Phenols and Phthalates from Dietary Intake and Personal Care Products: a Scoping Review
references.finding: Scoping review: interventions that removed sources generally lowered phenol and phthalate biomarkers within days, but compliance and contamination limited success, and policy may matter more than individual behaviour.

references.authors: Yang Y, Zhang F, Jiang Z, et al.
references.title: Microplastics are associated with elevated atherosclerotic risk and increased vascular complexity in acute coronary syndrome patients
references.finding: Blood microplastics (Py-GC/MS) were higher in acute coronary syndrome than controls and tracked IL-6 and IL-12p70; cross-sectional.

references.authors: Yuan M, Chai J, Song J, et al.
references.title: Association of bisphenol A exposure with in vitro fertilization outcomes: A meta-analysis and systematic review
references.finding: Higher BPA was associated with lower normal fertilization rates and fewer high-quality embryos in IVF/ICSI, but not with clinical pregnancy, blastocyst formation or implantation.

references.authors: Zhang C, Zhang G, Sun K, et al.
references.title: Association of mixed exposure to microplastics with sperm dysfunction: a multi-site study in China
references.finding: Raman microscopy found microplastics in all semen and urine samples; each additional polymer type detected was associated with lower sperm count, concentration and progressive motility; PTFE was singled out.

references.authors: Zhou Y, Lu Y, Luo Y, et al.
references.title: Associations between concentrations of microplastics in follicular fluid and the risk of diminished ovarian reserve
references.n: 25 women with diminished ovarian reserve, 20 controls
references.finding: Follicular-fluid microplastics (mainly PE, PP, PVC by Py-GC/MS) were higher in diminished ovarian reserve and correlated inversely with AMH and AFC.

references.authors: Zota AR, Phillips CA, Mitro SD
references.title: Recent Fast Food Consumption and Bisphenol A and Phthalates Exposures among the U.S. Population in NHANES, 2003-2010
references.finding: People getting at least 35% of calories from fast food had 24% higher DEHP and 39% higher DiNP metabolites than non-consumers; no dose-response for BPA.

audit.claim: Plastic particles are reported in blood, placenta, testis and brain and one NEJM cohort linked plaque plastic to 4.5-fold more cardiovascular events, but tissue numbers rest on a method prone to false positives and nothing shows that cutting exposure lowers body burden or risk (impact general 1, limited).
audit.biases: Measurement error and contamination: Py-GC/MS overcounts polyethylene and PVC in fatty matrices [ept-rauert2025, ept-almeida2026], and no human-tissue study met all essential QA/QC criteria [ept-lane2026]. Confounding and reverse causation in the plaque cohort (people with more plaque plastic may differ in many exposures); a single unreplicated cohort [ept-marfella2024, ept-marfella2024b].
audit.newer_evidence: No independent replication of the plaque-outcome association has appeared; newer studies are small cross-sections using the same Py-GC/MS approach, linking blood microplastics to acute coronary syndrome and inflammatory markers [ept-yang2024] and showing only moderate correlation between paired blood and plaque levels [ept-cui2025]. Methodological criticism has grown (2025-2026) [ept-monikh2025, ept-rauert2025, ept-almeida2026, ept-lane2026], and the brain paper was corrected [ept-nihart2025, ept-nihart2025b]. Published exposure figures check out against their sources (2.11 billion nanoplastics per cm2 in 3 minutes of microwaving [ept-hussain2023]; about 240,000 particles per litre of bottled water [ept-qian2024]; 11.6 billion micro- plus 3.1 billion nanoplastics per plastic teabag [ept-hernandez2019]; 39,000-121,000 particles a year [ept-cox2019]). Reproductive animal studies remain mostly of limited regulatory reliability [ept-due2026].
audit.bottom_line: Plastic particles have been reported in human tissue, but harm in people is unproven and the measurement method itself is under question.

audit.claim: Plastic is reported in human testes (mean 328 ug/g in 23 men by Py-GC/MS) and in most semen samples, with hints of lower motility in studies of 40-45 men, but the testis method is disputed and there are no human data on sperm DNA fragmentation (impact sperm 1, limited).
audit.biases: Cross-sectional designs with no exposure gradient; contamination and Py-GC/MS false positives for polyethylene and PVC [ept-rauert2025, ept-lane2026]; incompatible units across methods (ug/g vs particles); selection of fertility-clinic and varicocele patients; many polymer-by-endpoint comparisons.
audit.newer_evidence: Larger but still cross-sectional studies have appeared: 113 men in three Chinese regions (Raman; each extra polymer type detected went with lower count, concentration and motility) [ept-zhang2024]; 200 men (microplastics in 55.5% of semen; lower concentration only in a subgroup with frequent plastic-tableware use) [ept-qu2025]; 51 IVF couples (seminal PVC tracked lower motility, no effect on pregnancy) [ept-kong2025]; and a 98-man varicocele case-control using light microscopy [ept-ilki2026]. The earlier 45-man study's motility difference was p=0.056 [ept-guo2025]. The testis study's comment and reply stand [ept-hu2024, ept-uppu2025, ept-hu2025]. Still no human study of sperm DNA fragmentation. Follicular-fluid studies in women (44-51 patients) now report links with lower fertilization and ovarian reserve [ept-wang2025, ept-kong2025, ept-zhou2026], with the same method caveats; reviews conclude MNPs may be a reproductive hazard but cannot separate particle from additive effects [ept-wehrli2025, ept-due2026].
audit.bottom_line: Still a plausible but unproven sperm hazard: studies are bigger (up to 200 men) but all cross-sectional and method-limited, and no human DNA-fragmentation data exist.

site_change.headline: Plastic particles have been reported in human testes and in most semen samples, and cross-sectional studies of up to 200 men link them to slightly lower sperm count or motility, but measurement methods are contested, no study has a contamination-proof design, and there are no human data on sperm DNA fragmentation.
site_change.note: Add the 2024-2026 semen studies (Zhang 2024, Qu 2025, Kong 2025, Ilki 2026). Consider an egg-scope note or entry: follicular-fluid microplastics have now been linked to lower fertilization and diminished ovarian reserve in small Py-GC/MS and Raman studies (Wang 2025, Kong 2025, Zhou 2026).
